title: packet-ftp: Add support for exporting objects
description:
Add supports for exporting objects transferred
over FTP.

notes.body:
Image created with the PCAP from https://asecuritysite.com/log/ftp2.zip :

![image](/uploads/27cb3ac7a8bf7a70195205d1c24b766a/image.png)

Some potential ideas:
1) Should we support exporting objects that don't have a command? If yes, how would we combine files from multiple ftp-data packets?
2) Should we combine the working directory and filename to try generating a more user-friendly filename?
3) Is there anything sane that could be entered as the hostname or file type?

Updated picture based on feedback in comments:
![image](/uploads/06b3a5369697935c1e3e84950e88b359/image.png)
approved this merge request

approved this merge request
4. Should you rename the last column heading "Command"? :-)
Is that even an option?
Not sure if Guy was joking or not, but I would be inclined to show push RETR and STOR entries (i.e. actual file transfers, rather than including directory listings, etc)
I'm open to whatever the team prefers. I just don't want to spend a lot of time banging my head for features or functionality that is chosen to be scrapped.

This feature has been requested several times over the years, it would be great to have.  I do think that it should be limited to named file transfers, and that the filename should be just the filename (without the folder prefix) - it would be good to be able to show the server directory but there isn't currently a field/column to show more context around the file.

The tricky part is getting the stream re-assembled (and not offering the file for download if not complete).  tcp_dissect_pdus() might be one way - I don't know if the reassembly behind the TCP 'follow stream' tap would be available (if it is different from what tcp_dissect_pdus() does).

Other reasons why FTP export was never done might include:
- there is absolutely no framing of payloads, so you can - at a pinch - follow the stream and write the contents out to a file yourself
- when we (at my company) still use FTP, it tends to be for very large files, which might not be practical to allocate all-at-once in memory.  Your implementation constantly re-allocates the buffer as new segments arrive, which might become very slow.  So there might be reasons to want to switch off FTP file export or limit the size of files through dissector preferences?

I really would like to see this feature added - I wanted it a couple of years ago when I worked for a time with FTP (I added extra links/tracking around file transfers, server directory, but didn't get to the point of trying to do this).
@martin.r.mathieson : I created a preference to set a max file size (measured in MB). I set the default to 10 MB. Could you take a look?
Default is 0 MB (unlimited), but available to be changed, per discussion with Gerald Combs.

> 1. Should we support exporting objects that don't have a command?

What would cause that?  A capture that begins in the middle of a transfer?  A capture that included ftp-data packets but not ftp packets?

> If yes, how would we combine files from multiple ftp-data packets?

Without commands, I'm not sure there's anything other than a heuristic that will work.

> 2. Should we combine the working directory and filename to try generating a more user-friendly filename?

HTTP seems to use only the last component of the URL to generate a file name - and, on both UN\*X and Windows, I don't think / is a valid component of a file name, so, while it might be more user-friendly as a display column, it may not make sense to use it as the name to use when saving the file.

> 3. Is there anything sane that could be entered as the hostname

The server IP address, mapped to a host name if possible?

> or file type?

At most, you could guess it from the file extension.
It would be nice if we could use libmagic to check/classify all of the files available for export, but this is more general than this change.

For me, because we are not filling in hostname here, it displays multiple unprintable characters in the FTP-DTA object list window.  I'm not sure what the usual convention is for a file transfer, but I would think the IP address of the machine that sends the FTP-DATA frames would make sense?
I don't know how to do add the server's IP address or hostname - from what I could tell, neither of those are exposed to the FTP dissector.
You would know whether the command was STOR (client -> server) or RETR (server -> client).  And you do know the addresses of the FTP-DATA frames.

> And you do know the addresses of the FTP-DATA frames

How so?
pinfo->src and pinfo->dst

changed this line in [version 8 of the diff](/wireshark/wireshark/-/merge_requests/1611/diffs?diff_id=282412032&start_sha=e07443ab2272c9f7ac326bba13588a924e0f5f14#baaca25c73dd52cdad2a6adfc36ee79a8a424afc_201_220)

@martin.r.mathieson : Can you take a look - when I examined with a few passive FTP transfers, whether for a RETR or STOR, the correct origin for the file was always `pinfo->src`. This can be seen in the file mentioned earlier: https://asecuritysite.com/log/ftp2.zip.
I will try to take a look at this tomorrow Moshe.

I don't know what the expectation is, but when I added export support for TFTP I made sure that the file contents were complete, but here we are just appending them to the data stream regardless.  This could be useful, but also confusing (e.g. I ignored one of the data segments in a capture and was offered a shorter file for export).

Don't know how to work around that issue :(. My only guess would be to create some sort of upper-layer dissector that combines all of the FTP-DATA packets transferred into a single file, so that it can be easily examined and exported.

I don't know of an easy way to do this.  I saw Peter Wu's comments in https://gitlab.com/wireshark/wireshark/-/issues/14995.

I don't know if it'd be possible to trick tcp_dissect_pdus() into calling back a function with the entire reassembled tvb of the payload (i.e. ignoring duplicates, reordering and detecting the end of the stream).  As Peter says, I think sometimes you know the length before the data is sent.

As much as I like this idea, I think this goes into the territory of making it a far harder problem to solve, as there's no guarantee of any sort of 'closure' for a file transfer. I think it may be worth leaving that as a potential future enhancement.

changed this line in [version 14 of the diff](/wireshark/wireshark/-/merge_requests/1611/diffs?diff_id=286156176&start_sha=bcb6d8eba3284af716fa62b99a60cc77276df645#baaca25c73dd52cdad2a6adfc36ee79a8a424afc_168_165)
Complete. I also renamed the variable to more explicitly reference that.
Probably a comment here to say that you are appending new data to existing buffer.

I made it more explicit:
```
            /* This command packet number is already present in the
               command_packet_to_eo_row hashtable, so it's a continuation of
               a previous. Let's look up the entry in the export
               object list and append the data to there */
```
Does this mean the filename entry is still going to include the command as well as the filename itself.  I'd still prefer just to see the filename here, but don't feel that strongly about it.
Yes, it would include the STOR or RETR in the filename. I will parse the command to remove the command in the next iteration.

changed this line in [version 15 of the diff](/wireshark/wireshark/-/merge_requests/1611/diffs?diff_id=286156859&start_sha=c3e6bab016e1f7190b00d93d18b8d9d5e6c4f20a#baaca25c73dd52cdad2a6adfc36ee79a8a424afc_237_239)

Complete:
![image](/uploads/8422286828ef840b67956c1ca1ed0bc3/image.png)

We still don't have any guarantee that we're exporting ftp-data conversations that are complete, in-order and without duplicate data segments.  It may still be useful without this guarantee - what do others think?

I wondered here if the initial allocation should be bigger than the first segment.  I really don't know how quickly the realloc() function will grow the size (i.e. how many re-allocations will be needed to get to a reasonably large file size).

g_realloc() is currently called for each packet - there is no attempt at specifying additional, unneeded, capacity to attempt to reduce the number of calls.

~~Idea: What do you think about using a glib ByteArray to do that? https://docs.gtk.org/glib/struct.ByteArray.html~~

~~If you examine `g_array_maybe_expand()` there, it calls [`g_nearest_pow()`](https://gitlab.gnome.org/GNOME/glib/-/blob/main/glib/gutilsprivate.h) which "Returns the smallest power of 2 greater than or equal to n", or 0 if such power does not fit in a gsize"~~

~~As an aside, the only other change would be that it would need to use a second g_hashtable to store the mapping of command entries to ByteArray s, this time created with `g_hash_table_new_full()` at creation so that it could be passed a value_destroy_func of `g_byte_array_free()`.~~

~~EDIT: This would actually have a significant downside of doubling memory usage, because this would require keeping one copy of the data in the export_object_entry_t's payload_data and a second copy in the separate ByteArray - we wouldn't be able to have the export object entry's contents point directly to the ByteArray's storage because then we'd have a mess of them being free'd twice at cleanup. That extra cost and complexity leaves me still being in favor of simply calling g_realloc each time.~~
@martin.r.mathieson : Can I resolve this thread? I don't think there's anything more that we can really do here without drastically expanding the scope of this MR.

commits_data.title: packet-ftp: Add support for exporting objects
commits_data.message:
packet-ftp: Add support for exporting objects

Add supports for exporting objects transferred
over FTP. The max size for files to be
exported can be configured via preferences,
and is unlimited (0) by default.
